opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a question worth taking seriously instead of dismissing, because people moved on from GANs very quickly once diffusion models took off.

GANs have some properties that are still very attractive. The biggest one is efficiency at inference. A GAN generates an image in a single forward pass, while diffusion models, even with distillation, are fundamentally built around iterative denoising. GANs also have a very well-structured latent space. A lot of my earlier work, like interpreting the latent space of StyleGAN, showed that you can find semantically meaningful directions, such as age, pose, or lighting, and edit them in a fairly controllable way. That kind of disentanglement doesn't come as naturally in diffusion models.

The problem is that GANs are hard to scale. The adversarial training is a min-max game, so it's unstable, and the instability tends to get worse as you increase model size, data diversity, and resolution. Mode collapse is the classic symptom: the generator learns to cover a few modes very well and ignores the rest. Once you move from curated data like faces to open-domain, text-conditioned data at internet scale, that becomes a real bottleneck. Diffusion models, and now autoregressive and flow-based approaches, have a simple regression-style objective that is much more forgiving. You add compute and data and things reliably get better. That predictability matters more than anything when you're spending a lot of money on training.

So my honest view is that scaling GANs as the main generative backbone probably isn't the best bet for the field right now. The ideas behind GANs are far from dead, though. Adversarial losses are widely used in distillation to make diffusion models generate in one or a few steps, in tokenizers and autoencoders to sharpen reconstructions, and as discriminators that serve as learned perceptual metrics. In a sense the GAN has been absorbed into the modern pipeline rather than replaced.

If someone does find a way to make adversarial training as stable and as predictably scalable as the diffusion objective, that would be very valuable, because you'd get the quality and the speed together. I'd encourage people to work on that as a research question. But I'd frame the goal as understanding why adversarial training breaks at scale and fixing it, not simply making GANs bigger and hoping it works.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, Yujun Shen, in a conversational podcast style.

Honestly, I think the value is real but limited, and we have to be honest about why. My own research background is heavily in GANs, so I've had to think about this a lot. People saw diffusion models take off after around 2022 and said GANs are dead, but the first thing I'd push back on is that nobody actually tested that properly. Scaling GANs is hard for reasons that are not about data or compute. It's about training stability. The adversarial game is fundamentally a minimax optimization, and when you make the generator and discriminator very large, the dynamics become fragile. Mode collapse, oscillation, the discriminator overpowering the generator, all of these problems get worse rather than better as you scale. So there was a chicken and egg situation: nobody scaled GANs because they were unstable, and nobody fixed the instability because it seemed easier to just switch to diffusion.

Some work did try, like GigaGAN, and it showed that a GAN at around a billion parameters can still produce competitive images with a single forward pass. That's the key value proposition. Inference is one step, it's extremely cheap, and the latent space has a nice structure you can edit directly. If you care about real-time applications, interactive editing, or deploying on devices, that matters a lot.

But I'd say the honest assessment is this: diffusion and autoregressive models have a much more predictable relationship between scale and quality. You add compute, you get better results, and the loss curve tells you where you are. GANs don't give you that kind of signal. The loss doesn't tell you anything about sample quality. So from an engineering and investment standpoint, it's much riskier to pour resources into scaling a GAN.

So where I land is that scaling GANs as a standalone paradigm to compete with foundation models probably isn't the best use of effort. But the adversarial idea itself is far from dead. It's coming back as a component: adversarial losses in diffusion distillation, one-step generators trained with a discriminator, GAN-style objectives to make video models sharper. The discriminator is really a learned perceptual metric, and that idea will keep being useful no matter which generative framework wins. So I'd say don't scale the GAN, scale the adversarial idea inside whatever architecture turns out to be stable.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s worth exploring, but we should distinguish two questions: whether scaling can make GANs better, and whether it’s the most effective way to spend our resources.

For GANs, increasing model size and compute doesn’t automatically translate into better results. The generator and discriminator have to improve together, and training stability and diversity remain important. A model might produce very convincing images while still covering only a small part of the data distribution.

So I would evaluate scaling by what it actually unlocks: better quality, broader coverage, more controllability, and reliable training. GANs also have an attractive property: the generator can produce an image in a single forward pass. If scaling preserves that efficiency while improving capability, that could be valuable for interactive applications.

I wouldn’t dismiss scaling GANs, but I wouldn’t treat scale itself as the goal. The question is whether it gives us capabilities or efficiency that justify the investment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s still worth exploring, but we should distinguish scaling a model from simply making it bigger. The question is whether more data, more computation, and greater capacity continue to translate into better quality, diversity, and controllability.

For GANs, training stability is a major part of that question. If we increase the scale but the generator still misses parts of the data distribution, then size alone hasn’t solved the problem. We need to understand how the training process and the architecture should change alongside the scale.

So I wouldn’t dismiss scaling GANs, and I wouldn’t treat it as the goal by itself. I’d judge its value by what it enables: can we represent more complex visual worlds, give users more useful control, and retain efficient generation? Those are the outcomes that would make continued scaling meaningful.
